label: W0
name: Publish pipeline
scenario: You push a post in the study repo on Saturday. It must appear on buildwithvibs.in with no manual step, and never publish a draft.
concepts: why GITHUB_TOKEN pushes don't trigger workflows
core: Create the system-design-public repo. In the site's deploy workflow, check out the study repo and copy posts marked published into blog/posts before the build. Merge posts.json. Daily schedule plus a manual run button. Timebox: 4 hours.
breakIt: Push a draft (must not appear). Push two posts with the same slug. Run the deploy twice in a row: nothing should change the second time.
post: I've made 3 study plans and quit them all. Plan #4 is public, and it publishes itself.
read: GitHub docs: triggering a workflow from a workflow (the GITHUB_TOKEN section)

label: W1
name: QR core + menus
tag: Scan anything: the resolver and the first handler
scenario: One café's menu goes viral on Instagram. 5,000 requests a second hit a single code.
core: Code → resolver → handler interface. Menu handler on Postgres with Redis cache-aside. Hammer on one hot code, before and after caching.
breakIt: Flush the cache at peak load and watch the database fall over. Fix it with request coalescing.
post: One café went viral and my database fell over.
read: Scaling Memcache at Facebook (NSDI 2013): leases and thundering herds

label: W2
name: Drop
core: Checkout API with idempotency keys, a token bucket you write yourself, atomic stock decrement, a job queue for confirmations.
breakIt: Double clicks, client retries, kill a worker mid-order. Assert sold count is exactly 500.
post: How I sold item 501 (and how I stopped).
read: Stripe's engineering post on idempotency keys

label: W3
name: Load balancer
tag: Build your own, then put Drop behind it
scenario: Three instances of Drop. One dies at peak.
core: Round-robin HTTP load balancer in Node with active health checks, in front of three Drop instances.
breakIt: Kill an instance during a load test. Count failed requests, then add safe retries and count again.
post: I built a load balancer and finally understood TCP.
read: High Performance Browser Networking: the TCP and TLS chapters (free online)

label: W4
name: QuizArena
scenario: 1,000 players answer inside a 10-second window. The leaderboard updates live.
core: WebSocket rooms, a server-owned 10 s timer, a Redis sorted-set leaderboard, two WS nodes joined by pub/sub.
breakIt: Kill one WebSocket node mid-game with 1,000 simulated clients. Survive the reconnect storm with jittered backoff.
read: An engineering post on how Slack or Discord fans out realtime messages

label: W5
name: QR goes multi-tenant
tag: Gyms and cafés as tenants: attendance and forms
scenario: 200 businesses on one database. Someone screenshots the gym's QR and checks in from home.
core: Tenants with row-level security. Attendance handler with a 30-second rotating code. Forms handler. Signed webhooks with retries.
breakIt: Replay a screenshot, double-scan, read another tenant's rows, flood from one tenant and watch everyone else's latency.
read: AWS whitepaper: SaaS tenant isolation strategies

name: Moving to India
tag: Optional: one chapter a week. DDIA chapters on replication and stream processing.

label: W6
name: Footprint
scenario: Real traffic from your own blog, through a real event pipeline.
core: Tiny beacon on your blog → ingest API → Redpanda → consumer → column store → daily views chart.
breakIt: Crash the consumer, build a backlog, prove nothing was lost or double-counted.
post: I built analytics for my own blog with Kafka.
read: The Log: What every software engineer should know (Jay Kreps)

label: W7
name: Settle
scenario: Two people log the same expense offline, then reconnect.
core: Double-entry ledger, an outbox table with a relay to Kafka, a balances read model.
breakIt: Kill the service between save and publish. Does any money disappear?
post: Where did the money go? The outbox pattern, explained by breaking it.

label: W8
name: LLM gateway
tag: One front door for all your AI apps
scenario: Shared key, shared budget, and the main provider goes down mid-response.
core: Proxy with streamed responses, per-key token bucket, fallback provider, exact-match cache, cost log.
breakIt: Cut the main provider mid-stream. Does the user get a clean fallback or a broken answer?
post: Every AI app needs a gateway. I built one.
read: The Server-Sent Events section of the HTML spec

label: W9–10
name: LeaseLens
scenario: A 30-page Indian rental agreement. Flag risky clauses, with citations.
core: PDF ingest, hybrid search on pgvector plus full-text, cited answers, a 30-question evaluation set.
breakIt: Run the eval set after every change. Catch one confidently wrong answer and explain it.
post: My RAG was 80% right. Here's how I measured it.

label: W11–12
name: Judge
scenario: 300 submissions: clone, run in a sandbox, score against a rubric.
core: Queue of repos, a durable workflow (Temporal or Inngest), Docker sandbox with limits, rubric scoring, a review queue.
breakIt: Submit a malicious repo: a fork bomb, and prompt injection hidden in the README.
post: I let an AI judge 300 projects. Then I attacked it.
read: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting (Yao et al.)

label: W13–14
name: Recruiter agent
scenario: Many recruiting firms, thousands of CVs, streaming matches, under $15 a month.
core: Combine weeks 5, 6, 9 and 11. Deploy on AWS within budget.
breakIt: Full load and failure test, plus a recorded mock design interview.
post: My recruiter agent, end to end: the architecture.
